bio.en: Varun Parmar is Chief Product Officer at Miro and previously SVP and Chief Product Officer at Box, known for Miro's distinctive product culture.
bio.zh: Varun Parmar 是 Miro 的首席产品官（CPO），此前曾任 Box 的高级副总裁兼首席产品官，以 Miro 独具特色的产品文化而闻名。

summary.en: Varun discusses what makes Miro's product culture distinctive, how a visual-collaboration company scales while staying close to users, and lessons from leading product at both Box and Miro. He covers product-led growth, the role of craft and design, and how to keep quality high as a collaboration tool expands across enterprises. The episode is a practitioner's view of building beloved B2B products.
summary.zh: Varun 讨论了是什么让 Miro 的产品文化独具特色、一家视觉协作公司如何在贴近用户的同时规模化，以及从在 Box 与 Miro 领导产品中学到的经验。他涵盖了产品驱动增长、工艺与设计的作用，以及当协作工具向企业扩张时如何保持高品质。本期是关于打造受人喜爱的 B2B 产品的实践者视角。

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: Every single day, every single time somebody is pushing your code to production and you're releasing a feature or an enhancement, you are making the product better or you're making the product worse, but the products never remain same. So with every release that your competitor is making and every release that you're making, you are either making chess points, moves against them, positive points, or you're going negative. I think that framework, it actually drives an insane amount of clarity in terms of what you're doing and what the impact is going to be.
turns.zh: 每一天，每当有人将你的代码推送到生产环境，你发布一个新功能或改进时，产品要么变得更好，要么变得更糟——但产品永远不会保持原样。因此，每当你的竞争对手发布新版本，或者你自己发布新版本时，你要么在与他们的“博弈”中占得先机，要么处于劣势。我认为这种思维框架能极大地帮助你清晰认识自己的工作方向，以及所产生的影响力究竟有多大。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. A question I wanted to ask off the bat is just how has that cross-cultural approach to product teams impacted the way that you guys built product and the way the company operates?
turns.zh: 明白了。我首先想问的是，这种跨文化的产品团队协作方式如何影响了你们的产品开发和公司运营方式？

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: The one thing that's really interesting, Lenny, around the way Miro is set up is that our product organization is actually based in Europe and our go-to-market organization is worldwide. Our product management team, our designers, our engineers are located across three different hubs in Europe. What that sort of leads to is a couple of practices that we have as part of our culture. The first one is practicing empathy to gain insights. It's not just practicing empathy in terms of customers and figuring out what customer pain points and problems we can solve, but given our distributed nature in terms of having a global footprint and a lot of our go to market teams, folks in sales and marketing and customer success are in different continents or geographies, we have to make sure that we actually practice that internally. When we are interacting with folks, let's say in San Francisco, and those folks are out there meeting some of our large customers and stuff, how do we, in the product organization, understand their perspective, and bring that perspective into how we design, prioritize and build products? I think that's one thing that's unique. (00:06:43): I would say the other thing that's less to do with the location, but I think is sort of the core cultural value or philosophy that Andre, who's the founder and CEO has instilled in all of us, is practicing teamwork, how do we actually come together as a team, and bring down the silos that might exist across functions? I'll talk a little bit around how we are structured in the product organization so that it's a cross-functional perspective we bring to everything that we're doing because we believe the best work happens when we bring different diverse perspectives to the problem and then co-create the outcome that the customer is looking for.
turns.zh: Lenny，关于Miro的组织架构，最有趣的一点是我们的产品组织实际上设在欧洲，而我们的市场团队则遍布全球。我们的产品管理团队、设计师和工程师分布在欧洲的三个不同中心。这导致了我们文化中的一些实践。首先是通过共情获得洞察。这不仅仅是针对客户，理解他们的痛点和我们能解决的问题，而是考虑到我们的分布式特性——全球布局和许多市场团队分布在不同大洲或地区，我们必须在内部践行这种共情。当我们与旧金山的团队互动时，比如他们在那里与大客户会面，我们产品团队如何理解他们的视角，并将这种视角融入到产品设计、优先级排序和开发中？我认为这是独特之处之一。（00:06:43）：另外还有一点与地理位置无关，但我认为这是创始人兼CEO Andre灌输给我们所有人的核心文化价值或理念，那就是团队合作，如何真正凝聚成一个团队，打破跨职能部门可能存在的隔阂。我会稍微讲讲我们在产品组织中的架构，这样我们做任何事情都能从跨职能的角度出发，因为我们相信，当我们为同一问题带来多元视角并共同创造客户期望的结果时，就能产出最优质的工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to pull on these threads actually real quick. You talked about this value of empathy and the importance of having empathy across... because you guys are located in different locations and have different cultures, and also this idea of teamwork. What's something that you've done that helps you do that, either build empathy and maintain empathy across teams or make sure that people work in teams and not like, "Hey, there's this other team over there doing something else"?
turns.zh: 实际上，我想快速谈谈这些要点。你提到了同理心的价值，以及在不同团队和文化中培养同理心的重要性，还有团队合作的理念。你们团队分布在不同地区，拥有不同文化背景，那在这种情况下，做了哪些有助于建立和维系团队同理心的举措？或者说，如何确保团队成员能够协同工作，而不是各自为政、互不相让？

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: One of the most powerful things that I've seen work is the questions that you ask, the questions that you ask when you're going through product review or you are going to sit down and talk to someone and trying to understand why did they prioritize something over the other and was it something that was done through interactions they've had with folks internally or externally? I think it's the set of questions to ask in terms of how did they get to where they are today and was it informed by understanding of the insights that collectively the organization has? Was it informed by their understanding of where the market is evolving, where the competition is going. (00:08:31): Was it informed through the series of insights they have, either through inbound feedback that's coming through our different channels where customers are giving feedback or some outbound interactions that they've had? I think just trying to double click and getting to the details in terms of what insight led them to recommend certain things or make a left turn or a right turn is where I think is the most powerful way to make sure that those things are informed through practicing empathy internally and externally.
turns.zh: 我见过最有效的方法之一，就是在产品评审或与他人沟通时，通过提问来理解他们的优先事项——这些优先事项是基于与内部或外部人员的互动而形成的吗？我认为关键在于追问他们是如何形成当前决策的，这些决策是否源于对组织共识的深刻理解？是否源于对市场动态和竞争趋势的敏锐洞察？（00:08:31）是否源于通过多种渠道收集的用户反馈？或者是基于与客户的主动沟通？我认为深入探究这些细节——比如某个洞察是如何促使他们推荐某种方案、调整策略方向的——才是确保同理心在内外部实践中落地的最有效方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. There's this kind of cultural value of just assuming good intention and asking questions to understand where someone came from. I don't know if you'll have something off the top of your head, but is there a story or an example of that comes to mind where that was done well or not done well, I don't know, in something you recently were building?
turns.zh: 明白了。这其实是一种文化价值，即假定他人怀有善意，通过提问来理解他们的出发点。我不知道你能否即兴举例，但有没有什么成功或失败的案例，能说明在近期开发项目中如何践行或未能践行这种文化？

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: Maybe there are certain things, for example, anytime we're trying to build a new experience, one of the approach we want to take is very quickly validate that our original hypothesis, is that sound or not. We are big fans of the Design Sprint framework, what Jake Knapp has done I think is really amazing. In a short five-day window, you can get a small set of people to quickly mock up a concept, convert it into some sort of a prototype and then go out there and get some sort of a validation. Oftentimes when we are working on some of these new things, we have our product teams that are focused on zero to one initiatives, run this five-day initiative, and at the end of it we say, "Oh, this is great. Who did you get insight from?" There's a capability that we recently released, it's called Miro Talktrack, which essentially allows you to asynchronously do asynchronous collaboration by recording audio video on top of a Miro board. (00:10:16): We had two fundamental choices we could make. One, we could go down the path of what everyone's doing where you could do a screen recording and then spit out a series of videos, like pixels being captured. Or what we did was we actually went down a different path and the path that we went down was we basically synchronized the movement of the board. Let's say Lenny's presenting a board, some template he's created in terms of best practices for PMs, but he wants to have some sort of a talk track on top of it, an audio video feed. What we are doing is we're actually capturing the movement of the board that Lenny's going through along with the video talk track that's on top. The reason why we did that was because we had an insight that came through some of our interviews. (00:10:56): What our users want to do is they want to use Miro for collaboration. While communication is an important aspect of how teams come together, where we believe our sweet spot is that we want people to use Miro for collaboration. By making sure that they could actually use a video recording and while the video recording is playing, they could add in a sticky note, they could add in a comment, they could actually give a reaction. We were able to develop this insight by practicing empathy as part of the Design Sprint framework when we went and started to show our original concept and we walled and built on top of that.
turns.zh: 或许有些事情是这样的，比如，每当我们尝试打造一种新体验时，我们想要采取的方法之一就是尽快验证我们的初始假设是否正确。我们非常推崇Design Sprint框架，杰克·纳普（Jake Knapp）所做的工作确实令人惊叹。在短短五天的时间里，你就能召集一小群人，快速构思一个概念，将其转化为某种原型，然后去验证它。很多时候，当我们开发这些新事物时，我们的产品团队专注于从0到1的创新项目，开展这个为期五天的项目，最后我们会说：“哦，太棒了。你们从哪里获得的洞察？”最近我们发布了一项名为Miro Talktrack的功能，它本质上允许你通过在Miro白板上录制音频和视频来异步进行协作。（00:10:16）：我们有两个基本的选择。一种是走大家都在走的路线——你可以进行屏幕录制，然后输出一系列像素化的视频。或者我们选择了一条不同的路径，我们基本上同步了白板的移动。假设莱尼（Lenny）正在展示一个白板，一些他为项目经理创建的最佳实践模板，但他希望在上面添加音频视频反馈。我们实际上是在捕捉莱尼操作白板的过程，以及叠加在上面的视频对话轨道。我们这样做的原因是，我们在一些采访中获得了一个洞察。（00:10:56）：我们的用户想要的是使用Miro进行协作。虽然沟通是团队合作的一个重要方面，但我们认为我们的核心优势在于让人们使用Miro进行协作。通过确保他们可以在视频播放时添加便签、评论和反应，我们能够开发出这种洞察。在我们实践Design Sprint框架并开始展示我们的原始概念并在此基础上进行迭代时，我们获得了这种洞察。

I remember when Figma launched FigJam, there was a lot of just like, "Miro's dead. Figma's getting into the space, they're juggernaut, game over." Clearly that's not been the case and it just feels like, I don't know what it is internally that you all do that continues to allow you to compete and continue to innovate in the space. I'm curious just like is there something to how Miro approaches competition and also just, I don't know, the way they approach these sorts of challenges that is unique or interesting that you can share?
turns.zh: 让我们直接把他接入这期播客现场，跟我们讲讲Sprint流程是如何运作的。太棒了。这也与我之前想提的一个问题有些关联。你们所处的领域竞争激烈，Miro在在线协作白板领域确实走在了前列。然后在新冠疫情期间，随着远程办公需求激增，这一领域一下子火爆起来。“天哪，每个人都迫切需要这个工具！”这些年来，许多公司涌入了你们所在的市场，但Miro始终表现出色。我记得Figma推出FigJam时，很多人都在说“Miro死定了，Figma要进军这个领域，他们是巨头，游戏结束了”。显然事实并非如此，我很好奇你们内部做了哪些举措，才能在竞争中立足并持续创新。我很好奇Miro是如何应对竞争的，还有，他们应对这些挑战的方式是否有独特或值得借鉴之处？

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: If you look at the mission for Miro, we empower teams to create the next big thing and our focus is to enable teams that are innovating, and generally innovation happens at the intersection of a bunch of cross-functional folks coming together. Like we discussed, folks in product management or design or engineering or analytics or product marketing or research. What we find, Lenny, is that there are a lot of tools out there and those tools are generally sort of focused on a particular persona and maybe they're trying to solve the needs of a designer and a designer has a workflow that they're trying to do and they're using a specific tool and they sit at the adjacency of extending that core use case. The fundamental value that Miro provides is that we enable teams. I think what's unique about our product, and we can talk about the capabilities and roadmaps and use cases that we are investing in and we already have as part of the product, is that we take a team-centric lens. (00:13:50): So we're not saying, "Hey, we're building a tool that just works for designers," or "Hey, we're building a tool that just works for engineers." Because we fundamentally believe that innovation happens when cross-functional teams come together. When you look at the problem through that lens, you realize that you have to actually architect your solution. You have to think about the use cases and you have to go and prioritize certain experiences that are different and our customers see value in that, right? I think that's probably one sort of big macro aspect of how we think about our capabilities and products and why our customers think of us differently. I'd say that's say one point. (00:14:27): I think the second thing is Miro is actually used obviously by teams that are creating these innovative products and we actually have broad applicability across industries and verticals. While some tools might be hyper-focused on digital experiences and Miro's has great offerings there in terms of core capabilities, what we find is that Miro is used equally by companies in manufacturing, by companies in healthcare, by companies in architecture and engineering and construction functions, by companies that are in aerospace, governmental agencies and medical agencies and so on and so forth. I think the platform is actually much more agnostic in terms of its capabilities and what we offer that actually makes it more accessible and appealing to organizations that want to go beyond just digital experiences. (00:15:26): Then I would say finally there are capabilities that are available very, very uniquely to Miro that are valued by our users. That again is a big reason people come to Miro. For example, if Lenny's trying to conduct a big workshop with a bunch of product folks and he wants to facilitate that workshop and wants to have certain folks focus on one part of the board and while others focus on the other part, then there are some advanced capabilities that enable certain use cases like workshops. Or if you want to use Miro for some team rituals or from some agile practices, there are core set of capabilities that you could use the product for that are missing in some of the other capabilities. I would say a combination of all of those three things continue to drive differentiation. I would say on top of that, we are a big fan of our community and we believe that community love is what drives us. That's the fuel that keeps us going every single day.
turns.zh:
若审视Miro的使命，我们致力于助力团队创造下一个重大创新成果。我们的核心关注点在于赋能创新团队，而创新往往诞生于跨职能人才的深度协作之中。正如我们此前所讨论的，产品管理、设计、工程、分析、产品营销及研究等领域的专业人士共同汇聚，形成创新生态。伦尼，我们发现市面上诸多工具大多针对特定人群，或许试图满足某类设计师的需求——这些设计师遵循特定的工作流程，使用专属工具，并在核心用例的基础上进行拓展。而Miro的核心价值在于赋能团队协作。我认为我们的产品独具特色，无论是正在投入开发的功能模块，还是现有产品中的核心体验，都秉持以团队为核心的视角。我们从不局限于“专为设计师打造的工具”或“专为工程师打造的工具”，因为我们坚信创新源于跨职能团队的深度协作。若以此视角审视问题，你会发现必须精心设计解决方案，深思用户场景，并优先优化差异化体验——我们的客户正是因此深有共鸣。这或许是我们构建产品能力的核心理念，也是客户对我们评价不同的关键原因之一。

（00:13:50）第二点在于，Miro确实被众多创新团队所采用，但其适用场景远不止数字体验领域。我们为各行业、垂直领域提供广泛适用性方案。虽然部分工具可能专注于数字体验，Miro在核心功能方面也表现出色，但我们发现Miro同样深受制造业、医疗、建筑工程、航空航天、政府机构、医疗机构等领域的青睐。其平台能力的包容性，使得Miro超越单一数字应用场景，吸引更多组织客户。

（00:15:26）最后，Miro独有的核心功能深受用户推崇。这正是用户选择Miro的关键原因。例如，当伦尼需要组织产品团队大型研讨会时，他可以灵活配置会议板，让部分成员专注某个模块，而其他人则关注其他区域。此外，Miro还支持敏捷开发中的团队仪式，提供其他工具所缺乏的核心协作功能。三者协同作用持续打造差异化竞争优势。

除此之外，我们深信社区力量是推动产品发展的核心动力。正如伦尼所言，社区的支持是我们前进的不竭动力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Just to summarize and I was taking notes as you're chatting, just thinking about what allows you all to continue to do well in the market, considering all the competition constantly coming at you. One, as you mentioned, just there's kind of like a innate multi-functional architecture which is hard for someone to copy if they weren't built from that without the start. Two, it sounds like you are focusing on a wide spectrum of personas and it's not just tech employees basically. Also, just there's specific features that end up being really important that maybe people have a hard time building and then this last piece of the community. Awesome.
turns.zh: 太棒了。总结一下，您在聊天时我一直在做笔记，想了解面对激烈的市场竞争，你们是如何持续保持出色表现的。首先，正如您提到的，Miro具备一种与生俱来的多功能架构，如果不是从一开始就基于这种架构构建，其他人很难复制。第二，听起来你们正在关注广泛的用户群体，而不只是技术员工。此外，某些特定功能对用户至关重要，但其他公司可能难以开发。最后是社区建设。太棒了。

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's dig into the product team a little bit and understand how you all build product and structure product team. How many PMs are there at Miro? Then just broadly, how many employees, just to give people a set of, little bit of context?
turns.zh: 让我们深入了解一下产品团队，了解你们如何构建产品和组织产品团队。Miro的产品经理有多少人？然后大致说一下，员工总数是多少？给人们一点背景信息。

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: Give or take about 1,800 employees at Miro globally across all of the 12 hubs, and specifically in terms of the number of product managers, there are over 450 PMs in the team.
turns.zh: Miro在全球12个中心共有约1,800名员工。具体来说，产品经理团队有450多人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Then how's the product team structured? Is it like outcome oriented? Is it product area oriented? Is it user persona oriented? Is it something else? How do you think about the structure of the product team?
turns.zh: 那么产品团队是如何组织的？是以结果为导向？是以产品领域为导向？是以用户角色为导向？还是其他方式？您如何看待产品团队的结构？

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: Yeah, so I would say it's maybe a hybrid structure that we have, but the foundation of the team setup is around persona. We have what we refer to as streams, some companies refer to as domains, but essentially it's a set of individuals that are focused on solving the problems for a key persona. Just to give you an example, we have a stream that's focused on enterprise, and in enterprise we are looking at the IT admin persona, we're looking at the security persona or the compliance persona. There are a set of folks who are creating a roadmap and innovating for that audience. There's another stream which is called platform where we are going after the developer install base, folks that want to use Miro as a platform and build apps that they can actually make available either on the marketplace for everyone to use or they could be developers that are inside of a large organization and they're trying to integrate Miro with their specific use cases and workflows and business systems. That's another sort of stream that's focused on that, and there are a couple of other streams like that. (00:18:53): Then finally there are some just horizontal sort of streams, if you will. We have a big focus given that we are a PLG-led company around growth and self-serve business. We've got a stream that's actually focused on our core internal infrastructure. We've got a stream that's actually focused on data science that's doing all of the magic that we started to release in terms of Miro AI, et cetera, et cetera. I would say it's a combination of those. At the heart of it is we are focused on personas and we are sort of aligning people around solving problems and creating value for that persona.
turns.zh: 嗯，我会说我们可能采用的是混合型结构，但团队的基础是围绕用户角色展开的。我们有所谓的"流"（streams），有些公司称之为"领域"（domains），但本质上是一组专注于为关键用户角色解决问题的团队。举个例子，我们有一个专注于企业的流，在企业领域，我们关注IT管理员、安全或合规人员。有一群人正在为这些用户群体制定路线图并进行创新。还有一个名为"平台"的流，专注于开发者群体，他们希望将Miro作为平台，开发应用程序，这些应用程序可以在市场上供所有人使用，或者他们可能是大型组织中的开发者，试图将Miro与他们的特定用例、工作流程和业务系统集成。这是另一个专注于此的流，还有其他类似的流。（00:18:53）最后，还有一些横向的流。如果您愿意这么说的话。我们作为PLG驱动型公司，非常关注增长和自助式业务。我们有一个专注于核心内部基础设施的流，还有一个专注于数据科学的流，它负责我们开始推出的Miro AI等功能。我会说这两者相结合。核心是我们专注于用户角色，并围绕为这些用户角色解决问题和创造价值来组织团队。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is really interesting. One of the downsides of a persona-based approach I imagine is that features keep getting added that solve that user's pain points. What have you learned about keeping the product consistent and having a holistic perspective on the experience? How do you address Those challenges?
turns.zh: 真有意思。我想，基于用户角色（persona）的方法的一个缺点是，产品会不断添加新功能来解决用户的痛点。在保持产品一致性以及从整体视角看待用户体验方面，您有何心得？您是如何应对这些挑战的？

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: Architecturally, there are two sort of things that we have done that allow us to not pigeonhole ourselves into that specific way of working. I completely agree with you, you could lead to that. The first one is actually when we think about the product org, we call our org, it's called AMPED, A-M-P-E-D. This is actually going back to our earlier point, Lenny, we had around what's unique about the product culture, what's unique about Miro, and we talked about teams coming together, removing barriers or silos cross-functionally. AMPED stands for analytics, marketing, product, engineering and design. And everything that we do in the product org, when we say the product org, we actually don't meet product managers. We actually don't mean product managers, designers and engineers. What we mean by product org in Miro is this AMPED function. By having this cross-functional representation where product marketing team is deeply, deeply embedded inside of each of these streams, what we do is that we have different perspectives that come in where they say, "Oh, wait a second, did you think about the end user experience?" (00:20:49): If you think about the end user experience, you know have someone on the team that says, "Wait a second, did you actually think about the enterprise requirements or what's needed in the largest corporation?" I think the unique setup of bringing these cross-functional folks allows us to sort of course correct. The second thing is the ways of working that we have. We have these product reviews that happen. We generally classify anything that we are doing in terms of its complexity around a small, medium or high complexity, and anything that's being worked on is actually being shared with the entire organization. If it's something that's small to medium, it's actually shared with the entire product org. In fact, if you are non-product, you can actually subscribe to that Slack channel as well. Everybody sees what the product org is working on, everybody sees what the core hypothesis is, "What is the solution for that, what is the proposed design for it, how are we thinking about the capabilities?" (00:21:49): Then anything that's big actually goes through a formal process like a product review where there's a meeting and a bunch of us are in there and it's up to us, including the product leaders, to basically make sure that we are connecting the dots in terms of having a much more holistic perspective. I would say lastly, as Miro has sort of scaled the spectrum of companies all the way from a team that might have two or three people and might be taking out their credit card and using Miro for their own team all the way to a large corporation that might have 50,000, 80,000 employees, all of them are using Miro. We've come to realize that at some point the deep enterprise requirements need to be encapsulated in a set of requirements or best practices and we need to make sure that those get democratized across all of the feature teams. (00:22:36): When I'm thinking about building a new feature, I have a checklist in front of me where I can say, "Here are the 10 things that I need to think of that I need to incorporate early on in my thinking in the architecture, in the definition of the process, so that it doesn't come downstream." I would say that's an area where we're still working on and more recently we put more focus and energy and there's a product manager who's now leading that particular charter.
turns.zh:
架构层面上，我们采取了两种策略，使我们不必局限于某种特定的工作方式。我完全同意你的观点，你提到的方向是正确的。第一点是，当我们思考产品组织时，我们称之为AMPED（A-M-P-E-D）。这一点回到了我们之前提到的观点，Lenny，我们探讨了产品文化的独特之处，以及Miro的独特之处——跨职能团队的协作与打破壁垒。AMPED代表分析、市场营销、产品、工程和设计。在产品组织中，一旦提到产品组织，我们实际上不单指产品经理、设计师和工程师。我们在Miro所说的产品组织指的是AMPED功能。通过这种跨职能的架构——产品营销团队深度嵌入每个职能部门，我们获得了不同的视角。比如有人会问：“等等，你考虑过终端用户体验吗？”（00:20:49）；又比如有人会问：“你有没有想过企业的需求或大型公司的特定要求？”我认为这种跨职能团队的独特架构让我们能够及时调整方向。

第二点是我们的工作方式。我们会定期召开产品评审会。所有项目会根据复杂程度分为低、中、高三个等级，所有进展都会在全公司范围内共享。低中级项目会与整个产品组织同步分享，而高复杂度项目则会进入正式评审流程，召集相关人员共同把关，确保全局视角的连贯性。我想最后要说的是，Miro的客户群体涵盖了从只有两三人的团队，到使用Miro进行内部协作的大型企业。我们意识到，针对大型企业的深层需求需要形成一套标准化要求或最佳实践，并确保这些规范在所有功能团队中得到推广。

（00:22:36）当我构思新功能时，我会参考一份清单：“在架构设计和流程定义的早期阶段，需要考虑以下10个关键点，以避免问题在后续阶段暴露。” 这方面我们仍在持续改进，最近投入了更多精力，有位产品经理专门负责此项工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love all these details. This AMPED structure, I love that. There's analytics, you said product marketing, analyst marketing and then product engineering design. It's rare that you see marketing as a part of teams, as a leadership, kind of part of the leadership group. Do you have a sense of what impact adding that had on the team or where that came from? Or is that just historically been something Miro has prioritized, marketing and product marketing?
turns.zh: 我喜欢所有这些细节。这个AMPED架构真是太棒了。这里有分析、产品营销、分析师营销，还有产品工程设计。很少能看到营销被视为团队的一部分，视为领导层的一员，融入领导团队之中。你能否谈谈添加这部分对团队的影响，或者这是否只是Miro一直以来优先发展的方向——营销和产品营销？

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: This was done before I got here and I wish I could take credit for it, but I can't. I think this was the result of an observation, which is quite similar to what you're saying, which is while we might be developing a lot of the features and PMs or thinking bottoms-up in terms of what we are building, we might find that what we have built might not be able to capture the imagination of what we originally thought it would. A big part of that is how are you going to think about positioning, how are you going to think about competitive differentiation? How are you going to package it up so that the sellers that are out there are able to position it in a way that the customer, in this case the buyer, might be an IT professional, might a line business leader, can basically see the full vision of where we are going? I think by having product marketing as part of AMPED, we now bring that unique perspective that may be missing in certain teams. (00:24:24): PMs are more acting as product owners or more focused on core problem and solution but not thinking about positioning, because that's so important, especially when you're thinking about a market that we are increasingly in that there is competition there. That's one of the first things we started off with and that's top of mind for you as well, is that everything that we are doing has to be looked through that lens. One of the core philosophies that I have, Lenny, is that the success of a company is a direct relation of what the competition allows you to do. I feel like not many people talk about that, but in many cases in my professional career, and I've been at it for close to 24, 25 years, is that every single instance when I looked at a company accelerated their growth or there was a deceleration of growth, it was a direct relation to what the competition allowed you to do. Obviously, you have to do everything that you should be doing, but competition is the biggest variable that allows you to figure that out.
turns.zh: 这是在我加入之前就形成的做法，真希望能归功于我自己，但没办法。我认为这源于一个观察，与你提到的很相似。虽然我们可能开发了很多功能，PM们也可能自下而上地思考产品构建，但最终发现所构建的功能未必能激发用户想象力。这其中很大一部分在于如何定位产品，如何打造差异化优势，如何将产品包装成能让销售人员有效传达愿景的形式。毕竟，客户可能是IT专业人士，也可能是业务部门领导，他们需要能清晰理解我们的发展方向。将产品营销纳入AMPED团队，就是为了引入某些团队可能缺乏的独特视角。（00:24:24）：PM们更多地充当产品负责人，或者更专注于核心问题和解决方案，而非产品定位。这点至关重要，尤其是当我们面对日益激烈的市场竞争时。这一点是我们最先关注的，也是你最关心的——我们所做的一切都必须从这个角度审视。我有一个核心理念，莱尼——公司的成功与竞争对手的容忍度直接相关。我觉得没多少人谈论这一点，但在我近24、25年的职业生涯中，每次观察到公司加速或减缓增长，都与竞争对手的容忍度直接相关。显然，你必须做好该做的一切，但竞争是解开这个谜团的最大变量。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to hear more about your core product philosophies, but let me dig into the one you just shared. What you find is that the way you grow or stop growing is often a direct result of your competition. Is there an example of that that comes to mind? I'm guessing maybe Box versus Dropbox is an experience you had there, or if not, what's an example of that that you've experienced, to make it a little more concrete even?
turns.zh: 我想进一步了解你的核心产品理念，但先深入探讨你刚刚分享的观点。你发现增长或停滞往往直接取决于竞争对手。这方面有具体案例吗？我猜你可能在Box与Dropbox的竞争中有所体会，如果没有，能否举个具体例子，让我们更直观理解？

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: For those of us who've been in the collaboration space, and I've been doing collaboration and productivity apps for over 20 years, over two decades, at some point, you have companies like Microsoft that get really attracted to a space and you can see the trajectory of a business that's growing at a certain clip and then all of a sudden there's a competitive product that enters that has the might of distribution and the might of pricing, and that's just a direct example. I think I've seen that multiple times, first at Adobe where I was part of the document cloud business, clearly saw that at Box as well. (00:26:27): I think you can, in general, sort of look at every single category and you can say that there was a category leader and they were growing at a certain clip or a certain pace and all of a sudden there were a bunch of entrants that get in and what happens to your growth rate? It's all dependent on how strong is the competitor in terms of providing a good enough solution? That's one. The second is how strong is the competition in terms of their distribution outreach? Then the third thing is how strong is the competition in terms of the pricing and packaging?
turns.zh: 对于我们这些曾涉足协作领域的人而言——我从事协作和生产力应用开发已有20多年——在某个阶段，总会有像微软这样的公司对某个领域产生浓厚兴趣。你可以看到一家企业以某种速度增长，但突然间出现了一个拥有强大分销和定价能力的竞争产品，这只是一个典型例子。我认为我多次见证过这种情形，先是在Adobe，当时我是文档云业务团队的一员，在Box也明显感受到同样的现象。（00:26:27） 我认为，总体而言，你可以审视每个细分领域，都会发现存在一个市场领导者，他们以某种速度增长，突然间涌入一群竞争对手，那么你的增长率会如何变化？这完全取决于竞争对手在提供足够优质解决方案方面的实力有多强？这是第一个方面。第二个方面是竞争对手在分销推广方面的实力有多强？第三个方面是竞争对手在定价和打包方面的实力有多强？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I really like this discussion, especially because often the advice is, "Don't worry about the competition, just focus on the customer, it's going to be fine." Which what you're saying is that's not right, and I agree. What do you do with that in mind? How does that impact the way you build product or strategy? Is there some you could share that maybe tactically someone could leverage to how they're approaching their product strategy?
turns.zh: 我真的很喜欢这次讨论，尤其是因为很多建议都是：“别担心竞争对手，只要专注于客户，一切都会好起来的”。但你说这是不对的，我也认同这一点。考虑到这一点，你会怎么做？这会如何影响你构建产品或制定战略的方式？有没有一些策略可以帮助人们更好地规划产品战略？

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: It depends on who the competition is and what is their unfair advantage here. We talked about one specific competitor and I have a lot of respect for them, by the way, and I learn a lot from them every single day in terms of how they make bets and how they enter markets and stuff. At some point I'm going to write a book on them, I feel.
turns.zh: 这取决于竞争对手是谁，以及他们的不公平优势在哪里。我们谈到了一个特定的竞争对手，我对他们非常尊重，每天都能从他们身上学到很多东西，比如他们如何下注、如何进入市场等等。说实话，我觉得我迟早会写一本关于他们的书。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Ooh. We'll have to come back to talk about that.
turns.zh: 哦。我们得回头再聊聊这个。

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: That's right, yeah. I think it sort of comes down to how do you think about your unique place relative to all of these players, and in your customer's mind are they able to clearly understand what is the unique value that you deliver relative to everything else? Part of that is the unique capabilities you provide. Part of that is how you're packaging those unique capabilities to them, and making sure that they in their mind can see how you coexist in this overall sort of tech ecosystem that they might be investing in, to enable their employees or to enable them to operate. So I think it's sort of looking at that from that lens, yeah.
turns.zh: 没错，我觉得关键在于你如何在所有这些参与者中找到自己的独特定位，在客户心目中，他们是否能清楚理解你相较于其他产品所提供的独特价值？这部分取决于你提供的独特功能，取决于你如何将这些独特功能包装给他们，确保他们能在脑海中看到你如何在整个科技生态系统中共存，这个生态系统可能是他们投资的对象，目的是提升员工效率或优化运营。所以我觉得应该从这个角度去思考问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So what I'm hearing is be very clear about your differentiator and continue to invest there and then make sure your positioning is clear around why you're... just identifying, "Here's why we're different and we're not just a better or worse version of this thing" or "Here's why we're different" and making sure that's really clear.
turns.zh: 明白了。所以我的理解是，要明确自己的差异化优势，持续投入其中，并确保你的定位清晰，说明“我们为何与众不同，而不仅仅是现有产品的改进版”或者“我们为何独树一帜”，并确保这一点足够明确。

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: Exactly. I think the other thing I would say, there's another core philosophy I have, which is products either get better over a period of time or they get worse. Products never remain the same. I think you can take that philosophy to a bunch of things in life, but I'm going to take the lens of products, which is my core philosophy is every single day, every single time somebody is pushing your code to production and you're releasing a feature or an enhancement, you are making the product better or you're making the product worse, but the products never remain same. The lens for this, Lenny, is actually from a customer's perspective, from the end user perspective. The thing is that if you are a player where there's no one else in the market, that's one thing, so that's great. Kudos to you for actually identifying a blue ocean strategy and sort of executing to that. But most markets, most products, actually have either direct or indirect competitors that are available. (00:29:40): From the customer's mind, you're doing something, the competitor is doing something, so in their mind they're looking at these products and they're looking at these companies and they're saying, "Which is better versus not?" So with every release that your competitor is making and every release that you're making, you're either making chess points, moves against them, positive points, or you're going negative. I think that framework, if you have in mind, it actually drives an insane amount of clarity in terms of what you're doing and what the impact is going to be. Because every single move that you're making, the customer has that sort of in their mind, if not explicitly, implicitly that they're actually comparing these things. I think it brings a level of focus in terms of where you need to invest and why you need to invest and why this is going to make those decisions. (00:30:28): I think it allows at least for product leaders to make some high quality decisions around the bets that they're making and how they're going to play out in terms of eventual once the dust settles and the market at large is going to say, "I'm going to standardize on something and now I feel I need to go get it for everyone." Or "This is the tool that I want to use for this particular use case." That all of these decisions that you are making ladder up to that final sort of play that you have to do in terms of the market consolidation that eventually happens.
turns.zh: 没错。我想我还要补充一点，我秉持的另一个核心理念是，产品要么在一段时间内不断改进，要么逐渐退化。产品永远不会保持原样。这种理念可以应用于生活中的诸多方面，但我以产品为视角来阐释——我的核心理念是，每一天，每次将代码推送到生产环境、发布新功能或改进时，产品要么在进步，要么在退步。产品永远不会保持原样。这种视角，莱尼，从客户的角度来看，也就是终端用户的视角。关键在于，如果你所在的市场没有其他竞争对手，那当然很棒。为你能识别蓝海战略并付诸实践点赞。但大多数市场、多数产品实际上都有直接或间接的竞争对手。（00:29:40）从客户的角度来看，你在做某件事，对手也在做某件事。在他们看来，他们会将这些产品和公司进行比较，问“哪一个更好？”因此，每次对手发布新版本，你发布新版本时，你要么在积累优势，要么在落后。我认为，如果你牢记这种框架，它会极大地提升你的决策清晰度，因为你做的每一项决策，客户都会在心里进行比较，哪怕不是显性的，也是隐性的。这能让你更清晰地知道在哪些方面需要投入，为何需要投入，以及这些决策将如何产生影响。（00:30:28）我认为这至少能让产品负责人围绕他们的决策做出高质量的判断，以及这些决策在市场最终整合时会产生怎样的影响。届时，市场会说：“我要标准化某个东西，现在我觉得需要为所有人引入它。”或者“对于这个特定用例，我想用这个工具。”你所做的所有这些决策最终都指向市场整合的终局阶段。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is so interesting. Essentially what you're saying is that you find that being very close to and understanding the competition really well is really essential, versus this kind of the other end of the spectrum almost from just like, "Don't worry about the competition, don't pay attention." I like this point, metaphor of just like, "Are we moving ahead or further behind?" Is that where you operationalize that to track that? Then also just how do you not over-obsess with, "Let's just catch up, get more features," that kind of thing? How do you find that balance?
turns.zh: 这太有意思了。本质上，你的观点是，密切关注并深刻理解竞争对手至关重要，而另一种极端观点则是“别管竞争对手了，别关注他们”。我很欣赏这种观点，用“我们是在前进还是落后”来比喻，是如何将其具体化来追踪进展的？同时，如何避免过度纠结于“我们要赶上进度，多做些功能”之类的事情？如何找到这种平衡？

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: I'll be honest, I don't think we've figured it out. We haven't cracked the nut in terms of how to operationalize this, but I know you are way smarter than me on some of these things, so maybe we can-
turns.zh: 说实话，我觉得我们还没想明白。我们还没找到如何将这种理念具体化的方法，但我知道你在这方面比我聪明得多，也许我们可以——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Unlikely.
turns.zh: 不太可能。

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: ... partner on this and come up with something.
turns.zh: ……合作开发出解决方案。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: All right, that'll be something we work on. Any other product philosophies that you want to share? That was awesome.
turns.zh: 好的，这方面我们会再深入探讨的。还有其他产品理念想分享的吗？刚才真是太棒了。

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: This is all sort of related to it. It's like a string of pearls. I think there's maybe one more pearl we can actually thread into the needle right here.
turns.zh: 这其实都与此相关。就像一串珍珠。我觉得可能还有一颗珍珠，我们现在就能把它串进针里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's do it.
turns.zh: 那就开始吧。

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: Which is we talked about how do you ladder this up and stuff, and then the question is, okay, how do you know that everything that you're doing, is that in the right direction or not? Should you move slow and be much more mindful about the things that you're doing or should you move fast and make certain bets and then decide certain things and stuff? I think there are two views that are out there. My personal perspective on this is that what you want to do is that you want to be the first one to hit the brick wall. This is particularly true when you are in a market that is competitive. The reason for that is that if you consider yourself as an innovation-centric company and you believe that you are building experiences that fundamentally don't exist anywhere else and you're sort of paving the way for the rest of the folks to basically get inspired with how you are building these experiences, speed is the single biggest determinant, in my experience, in terms of who ends up being more successful versus not. (00:33:14): I don't know, maybe this is a little bit controversial where people say, Go slow to actually go fast." I think I have a lot of respect for that and there's certain areas you should do that, but when you are trying to figure out new experiences and stuff and you don't know if it's going to resonate or not, speed is something that you should accelerate for the organization. I think Frank Slootman talks about this a lot in his book and how can you accelerate? I think for me from a product perspective, the fundamental concept is can you be the first one to hit the brick wall where you have the learning faster than anyone else in the market so that you can decide, "Oh my god, the path that I was going was not the right path. I need to do 10 degrees west or I need to do 30 degrees east." I think as long as you're one or two or three steps ahead of everyone else in terms of uncovering or discovering those insights, then I think you can continue to be ahead of the pack in terms of building your product in business.
turns.zh: 之前我们讨论了如何逐步推进等问题，然后问题是，好，如何确保你所做的一切都朝着正确的方向发展？是应该慢慢来、更加谨慎地考虑每个决策，还是应该快速行动、先下注再调整？我认为有两种观点。我个人的看法是，你要成为第一个撞上南墙的人。尤其是在竞争激烈的市场中更是如此。原因在于，如果你自认为是一家以创新为核心的公司，相信自己正在打造前所未有的体验，为其他人铺路，让他们从你的经验中获得启发，那么速度就是决定成败的最关键因素。（00:33:14）：我不知道，也许这有点争议，有人会说，"要慢慢来，才能真正快速前进。"我对此很尊重，也认为某些领域确实应该这样做。但当你试图探索新体验却不确定是否能引起共鸣时，速度就是组织需要加速的关键。从产品角度看，核心理念就是：你要成为第一个撞上南墙的人，这样你就能比市场上任何人都更快地获取经验，从而决定，"天哪，我之前走的路是错误的，我需要转向西边10度，或者东边30度。"只要你比其他人领先一两步，发现并掌握这些洞察力，那么在产品和业务方面，你就能继续保持领先。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You're talking about urgency. I've never met a founder or a product leader who doesn't want their team to move faster. They're always encouraging their team, "How do we move faster?" I'm curious if there's something you've learned tactically about helping your team move more quickly. You mentioned Frank Slootman's book. Amp It Up is what it's called, by the way, in case folks want to check it out and he's big on just like creating a sense of urgency, constant urgency, and we'll link to that and share notes. But yeah, what have you found helps create urgency and generally helps your teams move faster other than just like, "Move faster, everyone"?
turns.zh: 你说的是紧迫感。我从未遇到过不希望团队加快行动速度的创始人或产品负责人。他们总是在鼓励团队："我们如何能更快行动？"我很好奇你是否有策略性的方法帮助团队更快行动。你提到了弗兰克·斯洛特曼的书。顺便说一下，那本书叫《Amp It Up》，如果大家想了解的话，我们会附上链接并分享笔记。但你有没有发现除了"大家快行动"之外的其他方法来营造紧迫感、推动团队更快行动？

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: My fundamental belief here, Lenny, is that every product manager... I can talk to product managers because there is reason certain ones, someone wants to be a product manager, because in my view it's one of the most thankless jobs, like you get to do a lot of [inaudible 00:35:10] and it's like, "Why you have to do this?" But it attracts a certain personality and that personality is driven by challenge and that personality wants to prove that they can solve this challenge and do something amazing. I think fundamentally the product persona actually wants to move fast. I think the reason why in some cases we are not able to move fast is because of roadblocks that we run into and those roadblocks can manifest themselves into technical challenges, they can manifest them in cells of organizational challenges, they could be priority challenges and so on and so forth. (00:35:52): My fundamental approach to solving that is to ensure that the product leads who are working on these capabilities can instantly raise their hand and call out that there are challenges that they are running into. Then the job of the leadership team, the product management team, is to essentially go and quickly resolve those issues. I think if you are able to resolve those issues, then what it does is it actually starts a virtuous cycle where you can actually start to see those wins. Once you see those wins, you actually create that courage to do more things. Maybe because you've seen how that specific roadblock was solved and you have a pattern matching that you've developed now, you can solve a lot of those things on your own and it's the next level of challenge that you now going to raise your hand. (00:36:41): What that does is it starts to build this organizational competency in terms of how you can figure out what to build. We all find these people in our organizations where there's someone somehow is able to do certain things in one-tenth the time that it would take a normal person. It's not that they are 10 times faster, it's just that in my observation that they've figured out which part of the core base they should build in versus not, who should be part of their team and who should not be, how they need to define that from a scope perspective, what does success look like, and it's the architecture of bringing all of these things together that actually brings that magic formula line in terms of "Hey, we are able to deliver faster."
turns.zh:
伦尼，我在这里的核心观点是，每个产品经理……我能和产品经理们交流，因为有些人之所以想成为产品经理，正是因为在我看来，这是一份最吃力不讨好的工作——你需要处理大量[00:35:10]工作，然后人们就会问：“为什么你要做这些？”但它吸引了一类特定的人才，而这种人才的驱动力来自挑战，他们渴望证明自己能解决这些挑战并创造惊人成果。我认为，从根本上讲，产品经理的角色就是要快速行动。我认为在某些情况下，我们无法快速行动的原因在于遇到的阻碍，这些阻碍可能表现为技术挑战、组织架构挑战、优先级冲突等等。（00:35:52）：我解决这些问题的基本方法是，确保负责这些功能的产品负责人能立即举手报告遇到的挑战。然后，领导团队和产品管理团队的职责就是迅速解决这些问题。我认为，如果能解决这些问题，就会形成良性循环，进而开始看到成果。一旦看到成果，就会激发勇气去尝试更多事物。也许因为你已经看到某个阻碍被解决，并且形成了应对模式，现在你就能独自解决很多类似问题，而接下来你要面对的挑战层次会更高。
（00:36:41）：这会逐渐培养组织在如何确定产品方向方面的能力。我们在组织中都能发现这样的人：他们能以普通人十分之一的时间完成某些任务。这并不是说他们速度快十倍，而是基于我的观察，他们清楚在核心基础上哪些该构建、哪些不该构建，清楚团队成员该加入哪些、该离开哪些，从范围角度清晰界定任务，明确成功标准。正是将所有要素整合起来的架构，成就了"我们能更快交付"的魔法公式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I really like this topic. What I'm hearing is one of the biggest roots of slowdown in a company and product development is blockers not being unblocked, and I always feel the same thing. I feel like a PM's number one job is to unblock their team because their job is basically make the most out of their team that they're marshaling towards some outcome. The way you do that is just figure out what's slowing them down. You just talked about this idea of a PM raises their hand to leadership, "Hey, we're blocked by this thing." Is there a process you've come up with there that helps you do that, it's connected to-
turns.zh: 我真的很喜欢这个话题。我听到的最大问题之一就是公司和产品开发中的拖延根源在于阻碍未被解决，我对此深有同感。产品经理的首要任务就是为团队扫清障碍，因为他们的职责本质上是充分发挥所调动团队的价值。实现这一目标的方法就是找出阻碍他们的因素。你刚刚提到的产品经理向领导层举手报告"我们被这个问题阻碍了"，这里有没有具体的流程可以借鉴？这与——

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: Yeah, I would say we are trying to sort of systematically ingrain this in the culture of the organization. We have a motto in the product org, it's very simple, single sentence, deliver customer value faster with high quality. That's it. Everything that we do, and when I say everything, everything, Lenny, from performance and reward system and measurements, everything is based on this one single statement and it has three attributes. The first one is deliver customer value, and we believe customer value is only delivered when customers use it. Anytime as a PM at Miro, when you ship something, we are looking at, "Well, what was the metric you were going to move and how much did it move?" We have some original targets that we can go back to. That's the first aspect of what we're doing, deliver customer value. (00:38:35): The second one is move faster, and there are certain cycle times that we are measuring across the organization. From the time you came up with the idea to the time that you actually pitched a solution to the time you actually shipped it, to the time we actually moved the metric, it's information that has been collected and is being made available to the organization. You can say, "Hey, if it was a small, medium or large, what's the average? What's the medium, what's the variance?" And you can say, "Hey, looking at this data, what can be improved?" That's on the faster aspect of it. Then the last one is around high quality, which is we want to build best in class collaboration experiences, so we are always getting inspired by what we find in applications and experiences that we see around us and we are saying, "Hey, when it comes to designing, sharing flows, we believe that these are the three apps that have best in class sharing flows when it comes to designing some synchronous capabilities like this. These are the best in class apps that we should look at." (00:39:31): We are always trying to make sure that we are benchmarking ourselves against that and we have our design team. On a regular basis, like when we ship stuff on a monthly basis, our design leadership team does a triage of everything that got shipped into high quality or not high quality. It's just like a binary function, and we're doing that and we're saying, "Hey, the reason why we believe it's not high quality is because A, B, C, D, E and we're making it available to other designers so they can actually start to build that telemetry in terms of some things are more subjective." But you can start to see some patent matching and say like, "Hey, this is what great looks like."
turns.zh:
是的，我会说我们正试图有条不紊地将这一理念深深植入公司的文化之中。我们产品团队有一条座右铭，非常简洁，仅一句话：以高质量更快地为客户创造价值。仅此而已。我们所做的一切——我说的是所有事情，莱尼——从绩效与奖励体系到数据衡量，一切都基于这条核心理念，且它有三个核心属性。第一是「交付客户价值」。我们坚信，只有当客户真正使用产品时，价值才能被兑现。在Miro担任产品经理时，每次发布新功能时，我们都会关注：「你们设定的指标移动了多少？达到了多少目标？」我们会回溯最初设定的目标。这是我们行动的首要准则——交付客户价值。

（00:38:35）第二点是「加速迭代」。我们在全公司范围内衡量各个周期时长。从构思到提出解决方案，再到最终上线，再到指标数据变动——所有这些信息都被收集并向全公司开放。你可以问：「如果分小、中、大三种规模，平均值是多少？中位数是多少？方差是多少？」你还可以分析数据：「通过这些数据，我们能优化哪些环节？」这就是加速迭代的核心。

最后是「追求卓越」。我们致力于打造行业领先的协作体验。为此，我们不断借鉴市面上优秀的应用与体验：在设计协作流程时，我们会研究哪些应用拥有最佳的分享功能；在设计同步协作能力时，又会参考哪些应用的同类功能最为出色。（00:39:31）我们定期对照这些标杆进行评估。每月上线新功能后，设计团队会对所有功能进行质量评估，判断其是否达到高质量标准。这就像一个二元判定函数：我们会指出存在的问题，如A、B、C、D，并将这些反馈分享给其他设计师，让他们借鉴。当然，有些判断会带有主观性，但通过不断积累，我们能形成共识：「这才是优秀设计的标准样板」。

有些东西是我在Box公司学到的，也启发了我们在Miro公司的一些做法；还有一些则是我们自主发展出来的。我们建立的路线图流程就是其中之一。这是关于不同团队如何规划未来工作方向的首要机制。我们采用的是滚动式的六个月路线图，虽然看起来时间跨度较大，但正如我之前提到的，我们有众多企业级客户。就我所知，大型企业最关注的是路线图评审环节。这类会议通常是我最喜欢的环节——与企业领导层坐下来，一起梳理我们的研发进展。

（00:48:41）我们制定的滚动式六个月路线图每三个月更新一次。前三个月的路线图完成度目标为80%，即80%的已规划内容能如期交付。接下来三个月的目标则降至50%，确保在快速交付价值的同时不牺牲灵活性。这种机制让产品团队能够根据客户需求、竞争动态以及大型语言模型等技术突破灵活调整方向，而无需担心客户或内部的质疑。所有这些都基于我们每年发布的年度战略框架。

（00:49:34）每年我们都会发布战略白皮书，内部全员共享，清晰阐述我们希望布局的核心方向、背后的逻辑、预期成果，以及这些方向如何与OKR体系及整体业务战略相结合。各团队以此为基础制定三个月更新一次的路线图。同时，我们赋予团队自主管理部分流程的权限，鼓励他们遵循最佳实践。若有特定需求，敏捷教练团队会提供指导支持。

（00:50:31）此外，我们还有一些独特的仪式。比如每隔一周的周五举办的“Miro Connect”活动。每个周五下午四点至七点或八点，阿姆斯特丹办公室的团队会聚集在一起。现场氛围像是创意分享会或推介会，人们手持饮料，背景音乐轻柔，各个产品团队轮流展示他们的创新成果。这种活动偶有神来之笔，但若能做好管理，其带来的协同效应堪称惊艳。
获取。（00:51:20）：我跟你说，有个团队当时在柏林总部做展示，他们说：“我们正在开发这个功能。”有个工程师走到那张桌子前问：“你们在做什么？” 团队描述道：“哦，我们正在尝试做这样的东西。” 而这位工程师恰好曾在前一家公司解决过同样的问题——他真的实现过这个功能。于是他问：“那你们打算怎么实现呢？” 坐在那里的工程师回答：“我打算用这种方法，大概需要三个月。” 工程师又问：“那你介意我来帮你吗？” 团队说：“当然不介意，多一个人多一份力量，快去吧。” 于是那个人放下手中的啤酒，说：“好吧，我玩得挺开心的，要回家了。” 接下来的三四个小时里，他把整个功能写了出来，还提交了投票请求。（00:52:10）：第二天早上，Miro Connect展会上那个核心团队的工程师看到投票请求，审核了代码后感叹：“哇，这个功能原本需要核心团队三个月才能完成，因为他们缺乏相关专业知识，结果只用了三个小时就搞定了。” 因为有位工程师恰好路过，说：“我知道怎么做这个，我能帮你们。” 于是他立刻行动起来。我们就是在努力创造这些神奇时刻。这种情况偶尔会发生，但我们确实有过成功案例，每次有机会我都喜欢分享。但这也是我们在运营理念上形成闭环的独特之处。

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: Yes, yes, yes. At Miro, we practice OKRs and it starts off at the company level, and then those company level OKRs are taken by the AMPED organization. Like we describe, it's the AMPED organization, and then we break it up and I would say we have refined it over the period of time, the two years that I've been at Miro. Early on we were doing OKRs on a quarterly basis, and I would say more recently we've actually evolved to six month KRs. What we found was that six month was the right cadence in terms of giving enough time for teams to basically push forward in executing these KRS and minimizing the "overhead" of doing replan every single quarter. We found that it was much more effective and efficient for the entire organization to do it on a six-month basis. However, we are doing traction on a monthly basis. So every four weeks, as AMPED, we are looking at our KRS for the AMPED organization on a monthly basis doing traction. However, the planning, the targets, are done on a six-month basis.
turns.zh: 好的，好的，好的。在Miro，我们践行OKR，首先从公司层面开始，然后这些公司层面的OKR会被AMPED组织接手。正如我们所描述的，AMPED组织会将其分解，我想说，在我加入Miro的这两年里，我们对其进行了优化。早期我们每季度做一次OKR，而最近我们实际上已经进化到六个月的KR了。我们发现六个月的周期更合适，一方面给团队足够的时间推进KR的执行，另一方面又能最大限度减少每个季度重新规划的「额外工作」。我们发现对整个组织来说，六个月的周期更高效。不过，我们每月也会做追踪。所以每四周，作为AMPED团队，我们会每月检查AMPED组织的KR进展。但规划和目标设定还是按六个月为周期。

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely. Maybe talk about what use Miro for, but then what else is in there? What do you use for task management, bug tracking, things like that? Design?
turns.zh: 太棒了。这正好引出了我接下来想问的一个问题——产品团队的工作流程中还用到了哪些其他工具呢？显然Miro是其中之一。你能讲讲Miro的具体用途吗？那其他工具呢？比如任务管理、缺陷追踪、设计协作之类的工具，你们都用什么？

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: Starting from the bottom-up infrastructure view, so all of our tickets are handled in Jira and we are using some of the newer capabilities in Jira in terms of coming up with roadmaps and coming up with the priorities and stuff. On top of that, all of the specs generally get recorded in Confluence. Having said that, we're actually a big fan of tools like Google Docs as well as Coda that allows us to track our KRs in a pretty effective way. On top of that, obviously we use Miro a lot, I would say for a lot of our things, especially on the product and design side of the team. Generally all of our insights get captured inside of Miro board, so when we are going and conducting user experience interviews and stuff, we will record those and then those recordings get added to a Miro board, so Miro access the content hub or a team hub for a particular project. (00:57:20): Once you capture all of those insights, then generally all of the brainstorming and team ideation happens on the Miro board as well, so Miro's actually also used as a tool to facilitate meetings and workshops. Once all of that is synthesized into a set of recommendations and outcomes, so when we go into these product reviews that we were talking about, Lenny, the same Miro board then gets manifested into a set of presentations, so we use Miro for presentations. We've actually made some really amazing updates in terms of our capabilities there and if folks haven't checked them out, I would strongly encourage them. There's a capability called Showtime that basically abstracts out the UI and lets people focus on the content, but do it in a way that it's interactive so everyone that's on the call can have reactions, can share their comments and leave comments while the presentation is happening without actually disrupting any of the flow for the user, so we use that a lot for presentations as well. (00:58:15): I would say more recently what we've started to do is that we've started to move some of our synchronous meetings into asynchro view. I talked about this Talktrack feature that we have, and a lot of teams, what they would do is that they would actually send you five minute, 10 minute Talktrack in advance and it's just a link to a Miro board, you click on it and then you just sit back and relax. Then you have this magical experience where you're sitting back and the Miro board is automatically moving because Lenny was recording it like that. Then you have the video play and then you can pause it anytime, you can add in your comments and stuff so that the next time when you meet, instead of actually providing context to everyone, those synchronous sessions are lot more deliberate and focused on driving outcomes or achieving consensus, so people are just focusing on the comments that were added as part of a async product review so that when they meet synchronously they can use that. Miro boards are used for that as well. (00:59:06): I would say now a lot of our dashboarding shows up in Miro boards now. We recently released data visualization capabilities around most popular VI tools. At Miro we use Google Looker a lot, so a lot of our dashboards are in Looker, and what you would typically find is that our analyst team and product teams will just grab a link to a Looker dashboard, put it on a Miro board, and it unfolds into a full visualization. Unlike a screen grab, you never have to go update it because right there on the Miro board, it's always updated and you can refresh that, so you basically have this experience where Miro acts as that single source of truth for a lot of the teams across the entire journey of product development where a single Miro board is meeting the needs of multiple use cases there.
turns.zh:
让我们从自下而上的基础设施视角出发。目前，我们所有的任务都在Jira中处理，并利用Jira的一些新功能来制定路线图、确定优先级等事项。此外，所有规范文档通常都记录在Confluence中。话虽如此，我们也非常青睐Google Docs和Coda等工具，这些工具能有效地追踪我们的关键结果（KRs）。除此之外，我们团队在产品和设计领域广泛使用Miro平台，所有洞察都被记录在Miro看板中。例如，在进行用户体验访谈时，我们会录制相关内容，随后将这些录音添加到Miro看板中，使其成为特定项目的知识中心或团队中心。（00:57:20）：收集所有洞察后，团队通常在Miro看板上进行头脑风暴和创意构思。Miro还被用作会议和研讨会的工具。当所有观点被提炼成一系列建议和成果时，我们会将这些内容转化为演示文稿，供产品评审使用。我们近期对Miro功能进行了重大升级，强烈推荐大家体验其中的Showtime功能。该功能能抽象掉UI界面，令用户专注于内容呈现，同时支持实时互动——参会者可随时评论、分享见解，而无需打断演示进程。（00:58:15）：最近我们开始将部分同步会议转为异步模式。通过Talktrack功能，团队可提前发送5分钟或10分钟的Talktrack链接，用户点击即可直接进入Miro看板，轻松参与互动。借助录制功能，演示过程可自动推进，参会者可随时暂停、添加评论，确保同步会议更高效地达成共识或形成统一意见。Miro看板同样适用于此类场景。（00:59:06）：目前，我们的大多数仪表板都迁移至Miro平台。近期我们发布了基于主流可视化工具的数据可视化功能。在Miro中，我们大量使用Google Looker，分析师和产品团队可直接将Looker仪表板链接导入Miro看板，实现全面可视化。与截图不同，Looker仪表板会自动更新，用户无需手动维护。Miro真正成为多项工作的单一数据源。
在整个产品开发过程中，各团队仅需使用一块 Miro 白板，就能满足多个场景下的使用需求。

turns.en: Then for the road-mapping, is that in Miro, each team's roadmap, or do you use something like Jira?

turns.en: Yeah, so I think we've got a couple of tools for road-mapping, and our observation is that while those tools are great for the unique needs that they're solving, we haven't found a universal solution for road-mapping. But I would say it is a problem that is not completely solved in terms of how do we actually bring these artifacts together at scale. (01:00:27): What we are starting to see, and this is actually a unique use case of Miro, is that we actually enable our entire field organization using Talktracks. What happens is that we have our entire roadmap published out as a Miro board for enablement purposes, so that that's a artifact that is approved to be shown to a customer. What you will see is that you'll see five or six recordings in there, and the leader for enterprise has done a five-minute recording on everything they're working on. The leader for platform has done that. The leader for end user experience has done that. The person who's driving some of our AI experience has done that. So you can go in and you can just click on that video and you can meet your needs by using Miro and this capability that we have.
turns.zh: 是的，我们有几个用于路线图规划的工具。我们的观察是，虽然这些工具能很好地满足各自独特的需求，但我们尚未找到一个通用的路线图解决方案。有些团队使用Miro进行路线图规划，他们会使用Miro中的看板小组件来实现这一功能。他们正在做什么？接下来有什么计划？后备任务有哪些？但我认为，在如何大规模整合这些成果方面，这个问题尚未完全解决。（01:00:27）我们开始注意到的一个独特的Miro应用场景是，我们通过Talktracks为整个现场团队赋能。具体做法是，我们将整个路线图以Miro看板的形式发布，以便于沟通，这是一个获准向客户展示的成果。您会看到里面有五六个录制视频，企业部门负责人会用五分钟的视频介绍他们正在进行的工作，其他部门负责人也如此操作。比如平台部门负责人、终端用户体验负责人，以及负责AI体验的团队成员都会这样做。您可以进入系统，点击这些视频，通过Miro及其相关功能满足您的需求。

turns.en: That's awesome. It sounds like each team can basically choose the tools they want to use. There's no standardized, everyone needs to use Jira or Miro for their roadmap. I like that.
