Question I always try to get to is how do you think about balancing new bets and innovation with maintenance and just general incremental work? Do you have some sort of philosophy as a product leader broadly, and then maybe at Miro specifically, of just how to balance investments in these two buckets and maybe three buckets, bugs, incremental work, and then just big bet? How do you think about that?
turns.zh: 太棒了。看起来每个团队都可以自由选择他们想用的工具，没有强制要求必须使用Jira或Miro来规划路线图。这点很棒，我也喜欢团队经常这样做。最后我想问一个关于产品组织的问题，然后再稍微转向增长策略，谈谈Miro是如何发展的，以及你们在增长方面有哪些经验教训。我一直想问的是，作为产品负责人，您如何平衡新尝试和创新与维护现有业务、渐进式改进之间的关系？您作为产品领导者，或者具体到Miro团队，是否有一些理念来平衡这两类投资，或许还有第三类，比如处理漏洞、渐进式改进，以及重大创新项目？您是如何看待这个问题的？

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: We have some rule of thumbs in terms of how we want to allocate our investments across these buckets. I would say a lot of it, Lenny, actually depends on the state of the team. There are certain teams that have more tech debt than others. There are certain teams that are actually working on some really big zero to one features than other teams, and so I think there is a variance. The standard deviation actually is dependent on which part of the spectrum that you're in, which is are you a team that we believe needs to create the next generation experience on the platform and hence we have to prioritize innovative work or are you the team that's actually so critical to actually meeting our objective around better board performance or any of the other things that we believe are important and hence we need to invest in those critical areas? (01:02:41): But I would say in general innovation versus not, varies on a spectrum of anywhere from 60 to 80%. I would say about 20 to 40% of the available capacity at any given time is either getting allocated to architectural initiatives. There's a technology roadmap that our CTO is driving that we believe is extremely important as the platform scales, and now as we have over 50 million people on the platform, so we continuously have to invest in making sure that the platform can scale. There are certain teams that probably have 40 to 50% of their allocation towards that because they're a critical part of the component. There are other teams that are maybe more end user focused and are more UI focused where that allocation is lower. But I think general rule of thumb is 20% is always a given, but it can go as high as 40 to 50%.
turns.zh: 关于如何在不同投资领域分配资源，我们有一些经验法则。我想说，莱尼，这在很大程度上取决于团队的现状。有些团队的技术债务比其他团队多得多，有些团队正在开发一些重大从0到1的功能，因此我认为存在差异。标准偏差实际上取决于你所处的阶段——你是需要为平台创造下一代体验的团队，还是对提升董事会绩效等其他重要目标至关重要的团队？（01:02:41）但总的来说，创新与否的比例在60%到80%之间变化。任何给定时间内，约20%到40%的可用资源会被分配到架构项目上。我们的首席技术官正在推动的技术路线图对平台扩展至关重要。如今平台已拥有超过5000万用户，因此我们必须持续投资以确保平台能够扩展。有些团队可能将40%到50%的资源分配到这方面，因为他们是关键组件的核心部分。而其他团队可能更侧重于终端用户体验，UI相关的投入则较低。但一般来说，20%是固定比例，但也可以上升到40%到50%。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: On bigger bets and longer-term thinking?
turns.zh: 关于大规模押注和长期思考？

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: Yeah, 20 to 40% goes on the technology-related initiatives and maintenance and stuff.
turns.zh: 是的，20%到40%用于技术相关的项目、维护等。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, got it. Infrastructure, maintenance, making sure everything's there. Got it.
turns.zh: 哦，明白了。基础设施、维护，确保一切正常运转。懂了。

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: [inaudible 01:03:44] Exactly, yeah.
turns.zh: [01:03:44不可听清]没错，就是这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Then what about just big, long-term bets that you're not expecting to pay off anytime soon? Do you have a heuristic of just what percentage of, say, total resources you put there?
turns.zh: 那对于那些短期内看不到回报的大型长期项目呢？你有没有一个经验法则，规定投入总资源的百分比是多少？

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: You've probably seen this, the framework of three horizon, it's quite popular in McKinsey and Harvard [inaudible 01:04:01] school and so on and so forth, is horizon one business, which is the thing that's delivering food on the table. Generally there's about a 70% allocation of resources that we have, give or take. Then there is horizon two, which is an adjacent thing. With the next 12 to 36 months we believe it's material. Usually that tends to be around 20% of the allocation. Then there's horizon three, which is three years out, three to five years, next generation things, and that's about 10% of the ratio. So it's like 70/20/10 across horizon one, two, and three.
turns.zh: 你可能见过这个，三重视野框架，在麦肯锡和哈佛商学院等机构很流行。一级视野是业务层面，直接带来收益。通常我们会分配70%左右的资源。二级视野是相邻领域，未来12到36个月内会产生重大影响，通常占20%左右。三级视野是三年到五年，下一代创新，占10%左右。所以一级、二级、三级分别是70/20/10的比例。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Any other thoughts along the lines of just how you think about product before we shift? I only have a few questions around the growth story of Miro and what you've learned about growing.
turns.zh: 太棒了。在我们转换话题之前，你对产品还有什么其他思考吗？我只想问几个关于Miro增长故事和经验教训的问题。

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: In terms of product leadership and what we believe is the way we want product leaders to be developed and I think it's more of a people philosophy. We have our product leadership which constitutes of all of the folks who are running all of these streams, and I always tell them that you have two personas that you have to think about. Everyone who's on the product leadership team is a product leadership team member. The fundamental thing that you have to do is drive accountability. The number one thing that a product leader on the product leadership team needs to do is drive accountability with others in the product leadership team. The other persona that they have is that they are a stream leader. They're actually responsible for delivering value for the respective persona and respective customers and stuff. So when you put on the persona hat of a stream leader, which is different than the persona or of a product leader, your number one metric, the number one goal that you have, is drive improvement. (01:05:42): When you go back and you work with your team, always have the lens are you improving things and whatever you want to improve, but you always have to ask yourself, "Today compared to yesterday, tomorrow compared to today, have I improved things? That's the yardstick you should think about. When you go sit in the product leadership team every Monday afternoon at 1:00 in the afternoon when we meet together, your number one goal is actually to drive accountability around this and are you making sure that we as leaders in the organization are doing the right thing for the company?" I think that's a philosophical construct that I always remind people in terms of what they should be doing. As an example, tomorrow we have calibrations, we have our annual review cycle happening in the company.
turns.zh: 就产品领导力而言，以及我们所认同的培养产品领导者的方式而言，我认为这更多是一种人才管理理念。我们有自己的产品领导团队，成员包括负责所有产品线的人员。我总是告诉他们，必须考虑两个角色定位。产品领导团队的每位成员都必须承担两个角色：一是推动问责制；二是作为产品线负责人，为各自的客户群体创造价值。当以产品线负责人的角色出现时（与产品领导者的角色有所不同），你的核心指标和首要目标就是推动改进。（01:05:42）：当你回归团队工作，始终要以改进为核心，无论你想改进什么，但你必须时刻自问：“今天与昨天，明天与今天相比，我是否有所改进？”这才是你应当关注的衡量标准。每周一下午1点开会时，产品领导团队的首要任务就是推动问责，确保我们作为组织中的领导者为公司做出了正确决策。我认为这是一种理念构建，我总是用它来提醒大家应当如何行事。比如明天我们要进行绩效评估，公司年度评审周期也即将启动。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Good times. Always a blast.
turns.zh: 真开心。每次都特别愉快。

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: Yes, exactly, always fun and so critical as a leader, because it sets the tone for everything that you're going to do. In my opening remarks, the only thing I'm going to remind everyone in the room is that "Your number one goal here is to be a product leader and accountability is what you have to write. That's it. Just hold each other as accountable, including myself in terms of making sure that as we go in, that's the key thing." I think once people understand the duality of how they need to operate across those two specific goals, it actually leads to really high-performing teams and teams that actually are able to create somewhat of a magic if they are open and there is trust that has been built in the team.
turns.zh: 是的，没错，总是很有趣，对领导者来说也至关重要，因为它为你接下来要做的一切奠定了基调。在我的开场发言中，我要提醒在场的每位："你们在这里的首要目标就是成为产品领导者，而问责制就是你们必须践行的。就是这样。彼此监督问责，包括我自己在内，确保我们朝着正确的方向前进，这才是关键。" 我认为，一旦人们理解了在两个特定目标之间保持平衡的重要性，这实际上会促成高绩效团队的形成——只要团队成员保持开放、互相信任，这样的团队就能创造奇迹。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When you say accountability, what does that look like? Is it pointing out, "Hey, you didn't achieve this thing we were trying to achieve" or "You didn't do a great job leading this meeting"? Is it just direct feedback often or is there some other way you see that manifested, and what do you like to see?
turns.zh: 你说的问责制具体是什么样的？是直接指出"嘿，你没有达成我们设定的目标"，还是"你没有把会议主持得很好"？通常是直接反馈吗？还是有其他表现形式？你希望看到怎样的表现？

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: Yeah, I think it's basically practicing feedback in a very open and constructive way and focusing on what is important for the business and not shying away from having some of those observations and conversations, not shying away from them. But it's all in the lens of what is the right thing to do for the business, and if you feel that that one or more members of the leadership team are not living up to what needs to be done, then just voicing it. It's not like you're complaining or anything, it's just like, "I have this perspective. Is this the right perspective or not?" Because actually it ties very well with the overall cultural values that we have. (01:08:02): If you do things with the lens that you are being empathetic, then you pose it as a question as opposed to a statement. I think that's one of the things that we practice a lot at Miro is that I believe that I am seeing there are certain things that are happening that it could be just me that I'm not seeing the other things. "But what is it? Can you help me understand? Can you help me figure out that why certain things are happening? Because I might just be missing the perspective." But because you bring it up, and that's part of practicing accountability in an empathetic way, it actually gets the entire team in the right mindset in terms of how they operate.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为这基本上就是以非常开放和建设性的方式进行反馈，关注对业务至关重要的事情，不回避提出这些观察和对话，不回避它们。但这一切都基于对业务最有利的考量，如果你觉得领导团队中有一人或多人没有做到应尽之责，那就大胆说出来。这样做并非抱怨，而是表达自己的观点："我有这样的看法。这是正确的视角吗？"因为这实际上与我们所秉持的整体文化价值观高度契合。（01:08:02）：如果你以同理心为出发点，那么你就应该以提问而非陈述的形式提出问题。我认为这正是我们在 Miro 经常践行的一点——当我发现某些正在发生的事情时，可能只是我个人的视角，而忽略了其他人的看法。"但具体是什么呢？你能帮我理解吗？你能帮我弄清楚为什么某些事情会发生吗？因为我可能忽略了某些视角。"但因为你提出了这个问题，这正是以同理心践行问责制的一部分，它实际上能让整个团队形成正确的运作思维模式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Has anyone given you some sort of direct feedback recently or pointed out something you didn't do well that held you accountable that you can share?
turns.zh: 最近有没有人给你一些直接的反馈，或者指出你做得不好的地方，从而让你承担责任，你可以分享一下？

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: All the time. Yeah, all the time. When we do our offsites, this is actually a fun thing, is that every offsite that I do with my leadership team, usually there is a one to two hour session where it is feedback to Varun, and I actually do it openly. I will have about eight to 10 people in the room and I will force people to be very honest and I want to show my vulnerabilities to everyone, that I am not perfect and I have lots of areas to improve. Every time people do it, it's interesting that they open up in very amazing ways and I think I love it because it helps me become better. It helps me identify my blind spots. But what it does is, because I do it in an open way, it brings a lot of trust. It brings trust that I do it openly and I'm an open book and they can share whatever they want, not just with me but openly in front of everyone.
turns.zh: 一直都有。是的，一直都有。当我们举办非正式会议时，这其实是个很有趣的环节。每次我和领导团队开非正式会议时，通常会有一到两个小时的时间用于给 Varun 反馈，我会公开地进行反馈。会议室里会有大约 8 到 10 个人，我会要求大家非常诚实，我也愿意向每个人展示自己的脆弱之处——我并非完美，还有很多需要改进的地方。每次大家这样做时，很有趣的是，他们会以令人惊叹的方式敞开心扉。我认为我喜欢这样做，因为它能帮助我变得更好。它能让我识别自己的盲点。但这样做的好处是，因为我以公开的方式进行，反而赢得了大家的信任。大家信任我公开透明，他们可以随心所欲地分享，不只是对我，而是公开地在所有人面前分享。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Are you willing to share one thing they suggested that they pointed out that they wish you did differently or better?
turns.zh: 你愿意分享他们提出的一个建议吗？他们希望你以不同或更好的方式做事。

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: Yeah, I think in general, finding time with me tends to be a bit of a hard thing, and generally there's always this feedback, which is need more time, maybe more responsiveness over email or Slack or something like that. That's an area that I'm constantly working on and improving, so yeah.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为总体来说，大家找时间与我交流往往比较困难，而反馈内容通常都是"需要更多时间"，也许是希望我能更及时回复邮件或 Slack 消息之类的。这正是我一直在努力改进的领域，所以是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That feels like a cop out. That doesn't feel too painful to hear. I'm like, "Yeah, yeah, I know. I don't have a lot of time. I'm sorry." But I get it, and that comes back to your point about blockers and how important it's to unblock teams because that leads to a lot faster progress.
turns.zh: 这听起来像是在推诿。听起来倒不算太难接受。我会说，"是啊，是啊，我知道。我时间不多。很抱歉。"但我理解，这又回到了你关于障碍以及解除团队障碍的重要性这一点，因为这能让团队进步得更快。

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: That's true, that's true.
turns.zh: 没错，确实如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so let me shift a little bit to Miro's growth and I only have a few questions here. I know it's getting late on your side so I don't want to keep you too long.
turns.zh: 好的，接下来我要稍微转向Miro的增长策略，我这里就只有几个问题。知道你们那边时间不早了，所以不想占用你们太多时间。

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: Sure.
turns.zh: 没问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The first is something I'm on this constant quest to understand how companies got their first users, and I haven't actually heard the story of how Miro got its first thousand users or customers. I know you weren't there in the early days, but you happen to know how Miro initially grew and got their first thousand users and customers?
turns.zh: 第一个问题是我一直在努力理解公司如何获得首批用户，但我还没听过Miro如何获得首千名用户或客户的故事。虽然你不在公司早期，但你是否了解Miro最初是如何增长并获得首千名用户和客户的？

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: I think the fundamental thing there is that we always had user first approach and reaching out to certain communities that were relevant to what was a key part of lighting the fire, if you will, the proverbial way people start to talk about the product. Given the collaborative nature of the product, some of the early adopters invited people who were also early adopters and the flywheel started to work. I've heard that we did a fair amount of content marketing and listing the product on sites like Capterra sort of helped. There was some early investments in terms of SEO and organic growth, so there was a focus there, which was the main source of driving traffic. The top of the funnel came through that. (01:11:43): The product teams were very intensely focused on building vital loops as a key mechanism of driving growth, once the traffic came in. Every interaction that actually introduced barrier, they looked at it and they looked at the data and they said, "Let's reduce this barrier. Let's remove this thing so that the product could be effectively embraced." It was an evolution over a period of time. There was also the fact that early on in the journey, some of the features were presented on a trial basis and then later on the model was evolved from a trial basis, time limited to a premium model that further accelerated the growth for the business. I would say those were some of the approaches that were taken to get to the first thousand users or so.
turns.zh: 我认为关键在于我们始终坚持以用户为先的理念，通过接触与产品核心相关的特定社区来点燃用户讨论热情。鉴于产品的协作属性，早期用户会邀请其他早期用户加入，形成良性循环。我听说公司做了很多内容营销，比如将产品上架Capterra等平台也起到了帮助作用。此外，在SEO和自然增长方面也早期投入了资源，这些都是推动流量的主要来源。顶部漏斗阶段就是这样实现的。（01:11:43）：产品团队在流量涌入后，高度专注于构建关键增长机制——关键循环。每当某个功能增加障碍时，他们都会分析数据并调整：“让我们减少这个障碍，移除这个阻碍，让产品更易被接受。” 这是一个逐步演进的过程。早期阶段，部分功能以试用形式推出，后来模式从试用转为付费，进一步加速了业务增长。我认为这些策略正是帮助Miro获得首千名用户的关键。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You talked about how Miro grows, where it has this magical loop of "I use Miro to for myself, then I share it with my team in whatever way I'm using it." They're like, "Oh, Miro, this is cool." Then they start using it and then they share it with people that they want to work with, and it creates this loop of growth." I imagine that's how Miro mostly grew initially and continues to grow. Is there anything surprising or unintuitive about how Miro grows that is beyond that? I imagine sales is a part of it and we can talk about that, but is there anything else that is interesting that is worth mentioning?
turns.zh: 你之前提到Miro的增长策略，即“我先自己使用Miro，再以某种方式与团队分享”，然后团队成员会觉得“Miro真酷”并开始使用，再分享给合作伙伴，形成增长循环。我想这就是Miro最初和持续增长的主要方式。除了这些，还有没有什么令人惊讶或出乎意料的增长策略？我猜销售也是其中一部分，之后可以再谈，但有没有其他值得一提的有趣之处？

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: No, I think that's the key of the growth. I think there are specific use cases where they are uniquely sort of geared towards inviting a lot of new people. For example, Miro is loved as a workshopping tool, and so generally one person is using Miro, but they invite 10, 15, 20, 50, 200, 300 people to that workshop. There are specific use cases where people get introduced to the product and then go and sign up for it and then start to use it for that use case or other use cases. I think the other accelerant in all of this is the templates that we have, in particular the role that Miroverse plays in all of this. (01:13:49): Just to give you an example here, there was a template which was created around FIFA World Cup, so there was a FIFA World Cup diagram. Cornelius, he's the founder and managing director of a Canadian strategic service design consultancy firm. He created this Miroverse template and it had over 100,000 views and about 15,000 copies were made of the single template. Given the popularity of all of this, it actually got indexed by Google. When you went in the search, you actually saw the Miroverse FIFA template show up when you were trying to search for FIFA World Cup, and that was another sort of acquisition channel top of funnel that actually drew a lot of users to it. So I think I would say the Miroverse is also a key accelerant to this.
turns.zh:
嗯，我认为这正是增长的关键所在。有些特定的使用场景下，Miro 产品本身就极具吸引力，能轻松吸引大量新用户。比如，Miro 被视为一个头脑风暴工具，通常一个人使用 Miro 时，会邀请 10 人、15人、20人、50人、200人、300人参与同一场头脑风暴。还有一些特定的使用场景下，用户接触到产品后会主动注册并开始使用，比如 Miroverse 平台的模板功能就起到了关键作用。

（01:13:49）我举个例子：有一个以国际足联世界杯为主题的模板，里面有世界杯相关的图表。康奈利斯是加拿大一家战略服务设计咨询公司的创始人兼总经理，他创建了这个 Miroverse 模板，该模板的浏览量超过 10 万次，单个模板被复制了约 1.5 万次。鉴于其受欢迎程度，该模板甚至被谷歌收录了。当用户搜索“国际足联世界杯”时，Miroverse 的模板会出现在搜索结果中，这实际上是吸引用户的首要渠道之一。所以我认为 Miroverse 也是增长的关键驱动力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If you had to think about the pie chart of how Miro grows, what percentage roughly would you say is word of mouth, organic, versus what you just described, which is essentially a CO versus sales, outbound sales? How do you think about that? Is there a way to model that simply?
turns.zh: 如果要画一张 Miro 增长的饼状图，你认为口碑传播和自然增长占多大比例？与你刚刚提到的以客户获取为核心、外向型销售的增长方式相比，比例大约是多少？你如何看待这种增长模式？有没有简单的方法来量化这一比例？

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: Without getting into specific numbers and stuff, I would say fundamentally Miro is a product-led growth company and product channels are one of the highest contributors for growth of users. As the business has evolved to serve the needs of some of the largest corporations in the world, the enterprise segment and the enterprise persona when they're trying to provision Miro for tens of thousands of users who then go conduct hundreds of thousands of workshops on Miro that invite millions of users on the platform, is a key part of the flywheel that we are seeing. I would say product channels are probably very strong and increasingly enterprise is a key part of that acceleration.
turns.zh: 不具体透露数字的话，我认为 Miro 根本上是一家产品驱动型增长公司，产品渠道是用户增长的最大贡献者之一。随着业务不断发展以满足全球大型企业的需求，企业级用户和企业客户在为数万用户部署 Miro 时，会举办数十万场研讨会，吸引数百万用户加入平台，这正是我们所见证的增长飞轮的关键环节。我认为产品渠道非常强大，企业级用户正日益成为增长的核心驱动力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A great segue to our final question, which is the idea that you started a product growth, sounds like clearly it's a big part of growth today, but as every product growth company does eventually you have a large sales team, I imagine, what have you learned as a product leader working with sales, especially at a product growth company about how to make that relationship work and have a product work effectively with a sales org?
turns.zh: 这正好引出我们的最后一个问题：你启动了产品增长战略，显然这在当今增长中占据重要地位。但像每个产品增长型公司一样，最终都会组建一个庞大的销售团队。我想知道，作为产品负责人，尤其是在产品增长型公司中，你在与销售团队合作时，学到了哪些让这种合作关系行之有效、让产品与销售团队协同高效的经验？

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: There are a few learnings and I would say maybe this is one area where we are working on how we could be doing better in terms of bringing ourselves closer to our high-touch and bringing high-touch closer to self-serve, in terms of how we operate overall. It's a lot of hard work, I would say first of all, basically, to bring both of these organizations together and you have to be very deliberate around the points of intersection and you have to make sure that these organizations don't consider themselves as competition. It's one product, one company, just two channels of how we are serving our customers. There's some things that we've done which is have the product marketing team that basically works across both of these functions and make sure that they are bridging what we are hearing from the sales organization in terms of what directly customers need on the enterprise side, and then what do we need on the self-serve side. (01:17:23): There's a full process in terms of how the handoff happens across the maturity of the account. It can start as a self-serve, it drives adoption, and once there's adoption, there's a hand raiser that happens and then there's a sales rep that gets engaged and you go through the qualification process and then you have an opportunity to expand the account. We've over the years sort of architected and built the entire funnel and what the process is, and that's also sort of a key part of how all of this operates. But like I said, I think there are a few areas where we could further streamline how we operate and think of it as one single unit.
turns.zh: 学到了一些经验，我想说，也许这正是我们正在努力改进的领域之一——如何让我们的高接触服务更贴近客户，同时让自助服务更便捷，整体提升运营效率。首先，这需要付出大量努力。基本上，要把这两个部门整合起来，必须精心规划双方的合作界面，同时确保这两个部门不会将彼此视为竞争对手。毕竟，我们是同一家公司，只不过采用了两种不同的客户服务模式。为此，我们采取了一些措施，比如让产品营销团队横跨这两个部门，确保他们能准确传达销售团队的需求——一方面是企业客户的实际需求，另一方面是自助服务用户的具体需求。（01:17:23）：在客户成熟度不同的情况下，交接流程也各不相同。客户可能从自助服务起步，逐步提高接受度。一旦用户接受了产品，交接流程就会启动，随后销售代表介入，完成资格审核流程，最终才有机会拓展客户规模。多年来，我们精心设计并搭建了整个销售漏斗体系，这也是整个运营机制的核心。但正如我所说，我认为我们仍有几个可以进一步优化运营流程的领域，最终将其视为一个统一的整体。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I imagine that is true for every company out there.
turns.zh: 我想这对所有公司来说都是如此。

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One maybe final question before we get to our very exciting lightning round. What are some features that people could look forward to that are coming with Miro?
turns.zh: 在进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，最后再问一个问题：Miro即将推出的新功能有哪些值得期待的地方？

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: We recently, about a month ago, announced Miro AI, the backdrop of all the amazing work that's happening around generative AI and large language models and stuff. I think it was really, really exciting to see all of the community enthusiasm around the use cases that we launch. So we're going to be taking it across the finish line and doing a general availability in the coming weeks and months. I think that's one big thing and we'll be adding more capabilities there. Just today we actually announced a bunch of really deep enhancements and updates around how Miro can be used for team rituals and agile practices. Now you can actually do retrospectives in Miro where you can have a private mode where while Lenny's typing his feedback during retrospective, nobody else can see it and then one click you can reveal it. I just saw some of the results of the feedback and it was rated as the number one feature people saw. (01:19:14): There's also some deeper integrations in terms of bringing an entire program board from Jira to start to do dependency mapping inside of Miro in a fun and collaborative way, to use this dependency mapping along with program board to start to do program increment planning, which is essentially scrum of scrums or big room planning that's happening. There's some really amazing capabilities that we've added there, which is on the backdrop of some of the updates we've made in terms of estimation of sprint story points and so on and so forth. Now there's a whole plethora of capabilities and apps that are available as part of the platform that allow you to have your entire team conduct your team rituals in Miro and you can automate certain things, you can streamline things, you can do certain things in async and then do the rest in synchronous ways, so I think that's been a big update as well.
turns.zh:
最近，大约一个月前，我们推出了Miro AI，它是生成式人工智能、大型语言模型等领域所有精彩成果背后的支撑平台。看到社区对我们推出的用例案例反响热烈，真是令人振奋。因此，我们将在未来几周至几个月内正式将其全面上线。我认为这是重大的进展，我们还将持续扩展其功能。就在今天，我们宣布了针对团队仪式和敏捷实践的多项深度升级。现在，用户可以在Miro中开展回顾会议，启用隐私模式时，参与者输入的反馈内容不会被其他人看到，点击一键即可公开。今天我刚看到反馈结果，这项功能被评为最受期待的新功能。

（01:19:14）此外，我们还深化了与Jira的集成，将整个项目看板引入Miro平台，以有趣且协作的方式开展依赖关系映射。借助这种依赖关系映射与项目看板相结合，用户可规划项目增量计划，这实质上是Scrum中的Scrum或大会议室规划的延续。我们还对冲刺故事点的估算等功能进行了优化。如今，平台上已涌现大量应用，助力团队在Miro中开展各类仪式，自动化流程、精简工作、实现异步协作与同步沟通的无缝衔接，这无疑是重大升级。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. With that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. I've got six questions for you. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 太棒了。至此，我们迎来激动人心的闪电问答环节。我有六个问题要向您提问。准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: All right, let's do it. What are two or three books that you have recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 那我们开始吧。您向他人推荐最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: One is, I love this, When Breath Becomes Air by Paul Kalanithi. It's one of those really emotional books that at the end of it, you might have tears in your eyes, but really, really amazing. We talked about Frank Slootman's Amp It Up, and then Satya Nadella's Hit Refresh. I think philosophically some of the things that we talked about today are inspirations that I found in some of these books.
turns.zh: 第一本是保罗·卡拉尼提的《当呼吸化为空气》。这本书情感真挚，读到最后你可能会热泪盈眶，但确实非常震撼。我们还提到了弗兰克·斯洛特曼的《Amp It Up》，以及萨蒂亚·纳德拉的《重启》。我认为今天讨论的一些理念，正是从这些书中获得的灵感。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's a recent favorite movie or TV show?
turns.zh: 最近你最喜欢的电影或电视剧是什么？

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: Ted Lasso. I don't know if it's a recent one or not, but something-
turns.zh: 《特德·拉索》。不知道算不算最近的，但有件事——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's a new season.
turns.zh: 新一季已经上线了。

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: Yeah, I've enjoyed a lot. I think it's a very positive and uplifting message. I think the performance is huge. It's humorous, the characters are well-developed, so I think overall it's a treat, at least for, me to watch.
turns.zh: 是啊，我特别喜欢看。我觉得它传递了非常积极向上的信息。演员的表演也超棒。剧情很幽默，人物塑造得也很丰满，所以总的来说，这部剧太棒了，至少对我来说是这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's a favorite interview question you like to ask?
turns.zh: 你最喜欢问的一个面试问题是什么？

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: I actually ask a math problem. For those of you who interviewed with me, I have this math problem, which is based on how Adobe created its first Creative Suite bundle. I was actually part of the team that came up with the pricing and packaging for the first Creative Suite post-acquisition of Macromedia. It's a math problem that allows you very quickly to figure out people in terms of their problem-solving skills. Usually I give that problem to people. I've given it to, I don't know, 700, 800 people, so I now have a very, very well established standard distribution of how long it takes for people, where do they get stuck and where they've gotten stuck, for those people I've hired, what evidence do I have in terms of using that as a framework in terms of them being able to solve things? So that's my favorite question.
turns.zh: 实际上，我要出个数学题。面试过我的人都知道，这个数学题是基于Adobe如何打造首个Creative Suite套件而设计的。我曾参与Macromedia被收购后首个Creative Suite定价和包装方案的制定。这个数学题能快速评估应聘者的解决问题能力。我通常会把这个题目给很多人做过，不知多少次了，现在我已经建立了一套非常完善的标准数据库，记录了不同人完成这道题所需的时间、遇到的难点，以及最终雇用他们的成功案例。通过这个框架，我能有效判断应聘者是否具备解决问题的能力，所以这是我最喜欢的面试问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So you're saying you've mapped back people that have done a certain way on the problem with their success and you've kind of found that it's a good signal of their performance?
turns.zh: 所以你的意思是，你能将完成这道题的人与他们的成功表现对应起来，从而发现这是一个衡量他们绩效的有效指标？

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: Yes. Not directly, but yes, correlation and stuff.
turns.zh: 是的。虽然不完全直接相关，但确实存在关联性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's amazing. That's one of the biggest problems with interviewing. You think you're asking all these amazing questions and it's such a good signal, you have no idea. No one goes back and is like, "Oh, this person sucked. This person didn't... " That's really cool to get that much data on that one question. Two more questions for you. What's something relatively minor that you've changed in how you do product development that has had a tremendous impact on your team's ability to execute?
turns.zh: 太棒了。这正是面试环节最大的难题所在。你以为自己问了所有精彩的问题，觉得这是个绝佳的评估指标，却根本不知道真实结果。没人会事后反思说“哦，这个人真烂，那个人不行……”能从一个问题中获取如此丰富的数据，真是令人惊叹。再问两个问题吧。你在产品开发过程中做过哪些相对细微的改进，却对团队执行能力产生了巨大影响？

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: We talked about some of that, sort of removing the roadblocks. I think having this motto of great customer value faster with high quality, just the simplicity of that and it's actually part of our evaluation rubric, it's part of how we measure ourselves and stuff. So I think just coming up with these simple concepts that you can rally the organization around, and I think it's still a work in progress, but something that I believe is leading to positive outcomes.
turns.zh: 我们之前讨论过一些问题，比如消除障碍。我提出的口号是“以高质量快速创造卓越客户价值”，这个理念简单明了，实际上它也是我们的评估标准之一，是我们衡量自身表现的重要依据。我认为制定这些能凝聚团队共识的简单理念非常重要，虽然这仍在不断完善中，但我相信它正在带来积极成果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Final question. What's your favorite Miro template?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题，你最喜欢的Miro模板是什么？

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: It's the FIFA World Cup actually. I am so fascinated with what was done. Yeah, it's the latest one, but I think there's a bunch of them in terms of retros as well, and I think... like your template as well.
turns.zh: 实际上是FIFA世界杯的模板。我对他们的设计太着迷了。最新一届确实很棒，但往届的回顾模板也很棒，我觉得……你的模板也不错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. We will link to all of those. Varun, this was amazing. Everything I expected and more, your team is as interesting and unique as I thought, and I am excited for people to learn from you and we're going to share a lot of links alongside this episode in the show notes. Two final questions, where can folks find you online if they want to reach out and learn more, and how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我们会把所有相关链接附在节目笔记里。Varun，这次访谈太精彩了。你完全符合我的期待，甚至超出预期。你的团队和你的个人魅力正如我所料般有趣独特。我期待大家能从你身上学到更多东西，我们会把大量相关资源分享给听众。最后两个问题：如果想联系你或者了解更多信息，哪里可以找到你？听众又如何能为你提供帮助？

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: Thank you, Lenny. It was a lot of fun. I enjoyed our interaction. You folks can find me online on LinkedIn. I think that's probably the best way to connect with me. I think in terms of one or two things I can ask everyone is that, one is if you are an existing Miro user and you use the product for something interesting, I highly encourage you to contribute it as a template as part of Miroverse. There's a lot of folks who use that and we would love for you to contribute there. The second thing is, I know a lot of product development teams, PMs and designers are big fans of you, Lenny, so those are also the users that use Miro. If there's anything we could do to make the product better, if there's things that you feel like we can expand the platform into, we would love to hear from you and just reach out to me directly over LinkedIn, direct message or connect with me there and yeah, and let us know. We're here to serve.
turns.zh: 谢谢你，莱尼。今天的交流非常愉快。我很享受与大家的互动。大家可以在领英上找到我，我觉得这应该是与我保持联系的最佳方式。接下来我想请大家做两件事：第一，如果你已经是Miro的用户，并且用它做过有趣的项目，我强烈建议你将其作为模板贡献到Miroverse平台。我们有很多用户会用到这些模板，期待你的贡献。第二，我知道很多产品开发团队、产品经理和设计师都是你的忠实粉丝，而这些用户恰恰是Miro的核心用户。如果大家对产品有改进建议，或者希望拓展平台功能，欢迎随时通过领英直接联系我，发送私信或建立连接，让我们共同进步。我们随时为大家服务。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Varun, thank you again for being here.
turns.zh: 太棒了。瓦伦，再次感谢你的参与。

turns.speaker: Varun Parmar
turns.en: Thanks, Lenny. Awesome.
turns.zh: 谢谢，莱尼。太棒了。

turns.zh: 大家再见了。非常感谢大家的聆听。如果觉得这期内容有价值，可以在苹果播客、Spotify或你喜欢的播客应用上订阅本节目。同时，欢迎给我们评分或写下评论，这对其他听众发现本节目非常有帮助。您可以访问lennyspodcast.com查看过往所有节目或了解更多信息。下期节目再见。
